title: Iron condors and butterflies
teaches: How an iron condor (a put credit spread below the price plus a call credit spread above it), an iron butterfly (both short strikes at one price) and a long call butterfly (buy one, sell two, buy one) are built, and how to quote their max gain, max loss (the wider side's width minus the credit, times 100, times contracts), breakevens, and the assignment risks that formula leaves out.

facts.quote: To construct a short condor, the investor sells one call while buying another call with a higher strike and sells one put while buying another put with a lower strike.
facts.claim: An iron condor sells a call and buys a higher call, and sells a put and buys a lower put.

facts.quote: It could also be considered as a bear call spread and a bull put spread.
facts.claim: An iron condor is a bear call spread plus a bull put spread.

facts.quote: All the options must be of the same expiration.
facts.claim: All four options in an iron condor expire on the same date.

facts.quote: Typically, the call strikes are above and the put strikes below the current level of underlying stock, and the distance between the call strikes equals the distance between the put strikes.
facts.claim: Usually the calls sit above the stock, the puts below it, and both sides are the same width.

facts.quote: Long 1 XYZ 70 call Short 1 XYZ 65 call Short 1 XYZ 55 put Long 1 XYZ 50 put
facts.claim: OIC's example iron condor: long the 70 call, short the 65 call, short the 55 put, long the 50 put.

facts.quote: The maximum gain would occur should the underlying stock be between the lower call strike and upper put strike at expiration.
facts.claim: The max gain comes when the stock finishes between the two short strikes.

facts.quote: In that case all the options would expire worthless, and the premium received to initiate the position could be pocketed.
facts.claim: Between the short strikes at expiry, all four options expire worthless and you keep the credit.

facts.quote: In that case either both calls or both puts would be in-the-money. The loss would be the difference between either the call strikes or the put strikes (whichever are in-the-money), less the premium received for initiating the position.
facts.claim: At max loss only one side is in the money, and the loss is that side's width minus the credit.

facts.quote: Upside breakeven = lower call strike + premiums received Downside breakeven = upper put strike - premiums received
facts.claim: The break-evens are the short call strike plus the credit and the short put strike minus the credit.

facts.quote: An increase in implied volatility, all other things equal, would have a negative impact on this strategy.
facts.claim: Rising implied volatility hurts a short iron condor.

facts.quote: The passage of time, all other things equal, will have a positive effect on this strategy.
facts.claim: Time passing helps a short iron condor, all else equal.

facts.quote: If an early exercise occurs at either shoulder, the investor can choose whether to close out the resulting position in the market or to exercise the appropriate wingtip.
facts.claim: After an early assignment on a short leg, you can close the resulting stock position in the market or exercise your long option.

facts.quote: In addition, the other half of the position would remain, with the potential to go against the investor and create still further losses.
facts.claim: After one side is exercised, the other half of the condor stays open and can lose more.

facts.quote: Should the exercise activity be other than expected, the investor could be unexpectedly long or short the stock on the Monday following expiration and hence subject to an adverse move over the weekend.
facts.claim: A surprise at expiry can leave you long or short stock over the weekend.

facts.quote: If at expiration the stock is trading near either shoulder the investor would face uncertainty as to whether or not they would be assigned.
facts.claim: With the stock near a short strike at expiry, you can't be sure whether you'll be assigned.

facts.quote: A short iron butterfly consists of being long a call at an upper strike, short a call and short a put at a middle strike, and long a put at a lower strike.
facts.claim: An iron butterfly sells a call and a put at one middle strike and buys a call above and a put below.

facts.quote: An alternative way to think about this strategy is a short straddle surrounded by a long strangle.
facts.claim: An iron butterfly is a short straddle with a long strangle around it.

facts.quote: The strategy breaks even if at expiration the underlying stock is either above or below the body of the butterfly by the amount of premium received to initiate the position.
facts.claim: An iron butterfly breaks even at the body plus or minus the credit.

facts.quote: The loss would be the difference between the body and either wing, less the premium received for initiating the position.
facts.claim: An iron butterfly's max loss is the body-to-wing distance minus the credit.

facts.quote: Combining two short calls at a middle strike, and one long call each at a lower and upper strike creates a long call butterfly.
facts.claim: A long call butterfly buys one low call, sells two middle calls and buys one high call.

facts.quote: The upper and lower strikes (wings) must both be equidistant from the middle strike (body), and all the options must have the same expiration date.
facts.claim: On a butterfly the middle strike is the body and the outer strikes are the wings, the same distance away.

facts.quote: MAXIMUM GAIN High strike - middle strike - net premium paid MAXIMUM LOSS Net premium paid
facts.claim: A long call butterfly's max gain is the wing width minus the debit; its max loss is the debit.

facts.quote: If the stock were below the lower strike all the options would expire worthless; if above the upper strike all the options would be exercised and offset each other for a zero profit.
facts.claim: Outside the wings at expiry, a long call butterfly is worth zero.

facts.quote: In either case the premium paid to initiate the position would be lost.
facts.claim: Outside the wings, the long butterfly loses the debit paid.

facts.quote: The strategy breaks even if at expiration the underlying stock is above the lower strike or below the upper strike by the amount of premium paid to initiate the position.
facts.claim: A long butterfly breaks even at the low strike plus the debit and the high strike minus the debit.

facts.quote: This strategy has an extremely high expiration risk.
facts.claim: OIC rates a long butterfly's expiration risk as extremely high.

facts.quote: It could also be considered as a bull call spread and a bear put spread.
facts.claim: OIC's long condor is a bull call spread plus a bear put spread.

facts.quote: The long condor investor is looking for a sharp move either up or down in the underlying stock during the life of the options.
facts.claim: A long condor wants a sharp move either way.

facts.quote: MAXIMUM GAIN (High call strike - low call strike) OR (High put strike - low put strike) - net premium paid MAXIMUM LOSS Net premium paid
facts.claim: A long condor is opened for a debit, and the debit is its max loss.

facts.quote: A short call butterfly consists of two long calls at a middle strike and short one call each at a lower and upper strike.
facts.claim: A short call butterfly buys two middle calls and sells one call on each side.

walkthroughs.title: Two credit spreads, one range
steps: An iron condor is two credit spreads on one stock: a put spread under the price, a call spread over it.
Picture it: sell the 65 call, buy the 70. Sell the 55 put, buy the 50. All four expire together.
The two you buy sit further out. Those are the wings, and they cap the loss on each side.
Slide both short strikes to one price and it's an iron butterfly. Either way, that's the seller's side, not our trade.

walkthroughs.title: What it can make and lose
steps: Put numbers on it: buy the 95 put, sell the 100, sell the 105 call, buy the 110. You collect 2.80.
Best case, the stock finishes anywhere from 100 to 105 and you keep the whole 2.80.
Worst case is one side's width, 5.00, minus the 2.80 you took in. That's 2.20 a share.
Only one side can lose at expiry. The stock can't finish under 100 and over 105 at once.

walkthroughs.title: The butterfly
steps: A long call butterfly is one, two, one. Buy a low call, sell two in the middle, buy a high call.
Say you buy the 95, sell two 100s and buy the 105. It costs you 1.25.
Pinned right at 100 at expiry, it makes 3.75. Finish outside the wings and you lose the 1.25.
Don't count on that pin. It can happen, but closing exactly on the middle strike is a long shot.

questions.q: A friend sells an iron condor for a net credit. Which two spreads is he actually holding?
choices: A bull put spread and a bear call spread
A bull call spread and a bear put spread
A short call and a short put alone
A short straddle and a long strangle
questions.answer: A bull put spread and a bear call spread
questions.why: A bull put spread and a bear call spread. Most of the time the put spread sits under the stock and the call spread over it. Both are credit spreads, so he gets paid to open it. The long options further out are the wings, and they cap his loss on each side. Swap in a bull call and a bear put and you've built the debit version, the long iron condor. That's the seller's side, not ours. We trade shares, but you should be able to read one when it shows up in the chat.
questions.lesson_line: Iron condor: a put credit spread under the price, a call credit spread over it. The wings cap both sides.

wrong.A short call and a short put alone: That's a short strangle or straddle. No wings, so nothing caps the loss.
wrong.A short straddle and a long strangle: That's the iron butterfly, with the short call and short put on one strike.
wrong.A bull call spread and a bear put spread: That pair costs money to open. It's the long iron condor, and it needs a sharp move.

questions.simple: A put credit spread under the stock plus a call credit spread over it. Both pay him, so the condor opens for a credit.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09: wrong notes B and C)

questions.q: All four legs of an iron condor expire on the same date.
questions.why: True. One stock, one expiry, four strikes. That's the definition of an iron condor, not a choice. The legs differ in strike, in call or put, and in bought or sold. Never in the date. Put one leg in another month and it's a different trade, and none of the condor math in this lesson holds.
questions.lesson_line: One stock, one date, four strikes. That's the condor.
questions.simple: True, one expiry for all four legs is part of what makes it an iron condor.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09: why no longer says the whole position settles at once)

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: On a butterfly, the middle strike is called the ___.
questions.why: Body. On a butterfly the middle strike is the body. The upper and lower strikes are the wings, and both must sit the same distance from the body. All the options share one expiry date.
questions.lesson_line: Body in the middle, wings on the outside, the same distance away.
questions.simple: Body is the name for the middle strike of a butterfly, and the two outer strikes are called the wings.

reasons: key rests on one cited fact (f31)

questions.q: A friend wants a long call butterfly with evenly spaced strikes. Which legs does he put on?
choices: Buy 1 low, sell 2 middle, buy 1 high
Sell 1 low, buy 2 middle, sell 1 high
Buy 1 low call, sell 1 high call
Buy a call and a put at one strike
questions.answer: Buy 1 low, sell 2 middle, buy 1 high
questions.why: Buy 1 low, sell 2 middle, buy 1 high, all calls, one expiry. The two calls he sells in the middle are the body. The ones he buys below and above are the wings, each the same distance out. You can also see it as a bull call spread and a bear call spread sharing the middle strike. Remember it as one, two, one.
questions.lesson_line: Long call butterfly: one, two, one. Buy the outsides, sell two in the middle.

wrong.Sell 1 low, buy 2 middle, sell 1 high: That's the short call butterfly, the mirror trade. It wants the stock outside the wings at expiry.
wrong.Buy 1 low call, sell 1 high call: That's just a bull call spread, two legs. The butterfly adds a bear call spread on top.
wrong.Buy a call and a put at one strike: That's a long straddle. It wants a big move, the opposite of a butterfly.

questions.simple: Buy one low call, sell two middle calls, buy one high call. Think one, two, one.

questions.q: Your buddy sold an iron condor last month. Where does the stock need to finish at expiry for him to keep the whole credit?
choices: Anywhere between the short strikes
Only at the exact middle of the range
Beyond either of the long strikes
Between a short and a long strike
questions.why: Anywhere between the short strikes. Close between the short put and the short call, and all four options expire worthless. He keeps every cent of the credit. Fidelity even counts a close right on a short strike, but assignment gets uncertain there. Past a short strike, one short option is in the money and he starts giving the credit back. When you look at one, find the two short strikes first. That's the range the whole trade lives in.
questions.lesson_line: Between the short strikes at expiry, every leg dies worthless and the seller keeps it all.

wrong.Only at the exact middle of the range: That's where a butterfly peaks. A condor pays in full anywhere between its short strikes.
wrong.Between a short and a long strike: There one short option is in the money, so he gives back part of the credit or more.
wrong.Beyond either of the long strikes: That's the max loss. One whole side finishes in the money.

questions.simple: Anywhere between the two short strikes, because there all four options expire worthless and he keeps the credit.

questions.q: Hold a long call butterfly to expiry and the worst you can lose is the debit you paid.
questions.why: True. Below the low strike, every call expires worthless. Above the high strike, they're all exercised and cancel out to zero. Either way the debit's gone, and that's the floor. Fidelity adds commissions to that cost. It's the same idea as when we buy a call: what you pay is your stop. You know the worst case before you click buy.
questions.lesson_line: A long butterfly's worst case at expiry is what you paid for it.
questions.simple: True, outside the wings everything nets to zero, so you lose what you paid and no more.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09: 'at expiry' added to the statement)

questions.q: At expiry, an iron condor can finish with both its put spread and its call spread in the money.
questions.why: False. Picture where the stock would have to be: under the put strikes and over the call strikes at the same time. Can't happen. So only one side can lose at expiry. That's why the max loss is one side's width minus the credit. When the sides differ, you use the wider one.
questions.lesson_line: Only one side of a condor can lose at expiry. That's why the risk is one side's width.
questions.simple: False, the stock can't be under the puts and over the calls at once, so only one side can lose.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09: unsupported paper-loss line reworded)

questions.q: Same stock, same expiry, same wing width. How does an iron condor stack up against an iron butterfly?
choices: Less credit, a wider profit range
More credit and a wider profit range
More credit, a narrower range
Less credit, a narrower range
questions.answer: Less credit, a wider profit range
questions.why: Less credit, a wider profit range. The condor splits its short strikes apart, so the stock gets room and the break-evens sit further out. The butterfly sells both shorts at one strike. More premium comes in, but the stock has to finish close to that strike. With the same wings, the condor's smaller credit also means a higher max loss. You're trading premium for room. You don't get both.
questions.lesson_line: The iron butterfly pays more but needs the stock pinned close. The condor pays less and gives it room.

wrong.More credit, a narrower range: That's the iron butterfly, both shorts on one strike.
wrong.Less credit, a narrower range: Splitting the short strikes widens the range. The condor's break-evens sit further out.
wrong.More credit and a wider profit range: You don't get both. More room for the stock means less premium coming in.

questions.simple: The condor takes in less premium but gives the stock a wider range to finish in.

questions.q: A friend sells 2 iron condors at a 1.40 credit each. What's the most he can make on the trade?
questions.why: $280, and only if the stock finishes between the short strikes. The credit is the most a condor can ever pay. Each contract covers 100 shares. 1.40 times 100 is 140 a condor. Times 2 condors is 280. Commissions come out of that. Here's how I'd look at it. The win is small and capped, so check the max loss before the 280 gets you excited.
questions.lesson_line: A condor's best case is the credit, times 100, times the contracts. Small and capped.
questions.simple: $280, because the credit is the max, and each of the 2 contracts covers 100 shares.

wrong.$2.80: Forgets that each contract covers 100 shares.
wrong.$2,800: A decimal slip on the 100 shares.

questions.q: Your buddy's condor: long 45 put, short 50 put, short 60 call, long 65 call, for a 1.60 credit. Max loss per share?
questions.why: $3.40 a share. The worst case is the stock finishing past a long strike. Then one side is fully in the money and the other expires worthless. Both sides are 5 wide here: 65 minus 60 is 5, and 50 minus 45 is 5. Take the 1.60 credit off the 5 and you're at 3.40. So he's putting up 3.40 to make 1.60. That's the deal on every condor. Know it cold before a credit ever looks easy to you.
questions.lesson_line: Condor max loss: one side's width minus the credit, per share.
questions.simple: $3.40, because at worst one full side is lost, less the 1.60 credit.

wrong.$5.00: That's the full width. He keeps the 1.60 credit, so take it off.
wrong.$6.60: Adds the credit to the width. The credit cuts the loss.
wrong.$1.60: That's the credit, the most he can make. Not the loss.

questions.q: A guy in the chat lives on condors that pay small credits. What cost hits him on every open and every close?
choices: Bid-ask spreads on all four legs
Time decay on the two short options
The cost of the two long wings
One fee, since all four go in one order
questions.answer: Bid-ask spreads on all four legs
questions.why: The bid-ask spreads on all four legs. He crosses four of them to get in and four more to get out, plus commissions. Putting all four legs in one order doesn't merge those costs. Each leg still pays its own spread. And one condor only makes a small dollar profit to begin with, so the costs take a real bite. If you ever look at one of these, count the spreads against the credit first. A small win shrinks fast.
questions.lesson_line: Four legs, four spreads each way, plus commissions. Count them against the credit.

wrong.Time decay on the two short options: Decay changes what the options are worth. It's not a fee you pay to get in or out.
wrong.The cost of the two long wings: The wings are part of the trade, not a cost to trade it. The credit he sees is already net of them.
wrong.One fee, since all four go in one order: One order, four legs, four spreads. Each leg carries its own cost.

questions.simple: Bid-ask spreads on all four legs, paid going in and again coming out, and they eat into a small profit.

questions.q: A fund sells the 80 put and the 90 call, with wings at 75 and 95, for a 1.85 credit. Where's the upper break-even at expiry?
questions.why: $91.85. The upper break-even is the short call plus the credit: 90 plus 1.85 is 91.85. The stock can run past 90 by the full credit before the fund loses a dime. The lower one works the same way off the short put: 80 minus 1.85 is 78.15. The wings at 75 and 95 don't move either break-even. They only cap the loss.
questions.lesson_line: Condor break-evens: short call plus the credit up top, short put minus the credit below.
questions.simple: $91.85, because the stock has to clear the short call by the full credit before the fund starts losing.

wrong.$88.15: Takes the credit off the short call. On the upside you add it.
wrong.$78.15: That's the lower break-even, off the 80 put.
wrong.$90.00: That's just the short call. The credit buys another 1.85 of room.

questions.story: A friend's stock is at 50. He sells the 50 call and the 50 put, and buys the 45 put and the 55 call. He collects 3.20.
questions.q: Where are his two break-evens at expiry?
questions.why: 46.80 and 53.20. Both shorts sit on the 50, so it's an iron butterfly, and the 50 is the body. It breaks even the full credit away on each side. 50 minus 3.20 is 46.80. 50 plus 3.20 is 53.20. Inside that range he makes money, and the most comes with the stock right at 50. Past the wings at 45 and 55, the loss stops growing.
questions.lesson_line: Iron butterfly break-evens: the body, plus or minus the whole credit.

wrong.45.00 and 55.00: Those are the wings, where the max loss starts. The break-evens sit inside them.
wrong.41.80 and 58.20: That measures the credit off the wings. Measure from the body, the 50.
wrong.48.40 and 51.60: That splits the credit in half. The whole 3.20 covers each side.

questions.simple: 46.80 and 53.20, because an iron butterfly breaks even the full 3.20 credit either side of the 50 strike.

questions.q: Your buddy buys one 40 call, sells two 45 calls and buys one 50 call, for 1.10. Max profit per share at expiry?
questions.why: $3.90 a share, and only with the stock right on 45 at expiry. At 45, the 40 call is worth 45 minus 40, which is 5. The two 45s and the 50 call expire worthless. Take off the 1.10 he paid and it's 3.90. Anywhere else pays less, and outside the wings he loses the 1.10. Landing exactly on 45 is rare, so don't plan around that number.
questions.lesson_line: Long butterfly max: one wing's width minus the debit, and only right at the body.
questions.simple: $3.90, because at exactly 45 only the 40 call is worth anything, and he paid 1.10 for the whole thing.

deeper.trap: Don't use the whole 40-to-50 span. The Options Industry Council's formula uses one wing: the high strike minus the middle strike, less the debit.

wrong.$8.90: Uses the whole 40-to-50 span. One wing sets the max.
wrong.$5.00: That's the wing width. He still paid 1.10.
wrong.$6.10: Adds the 1.10 instead of taking it off.

questions.q: A fund sells 3 condors: long 95 put, short 100 put, short 110 call, long 120 call. Credit 2.50 each. What's the max loss?
questions.why: $2,250. The sides aren't the same width here. The puts run 95 to 100, the calls 110 to 120. Only one side can lose at expiry, so the wider call side sets the worst case. 120 minus 110 is 10. Take off the 2.50 credit and it's 7.50 a share. Times 100 is 750 a condor. Times 3 condors is 2,250. Whenever you check one, find the wider side first.
questions.lesson_line: Uneven sides, the wider one sets the max loss. Find it first.
questions.simple: $2,250, because the wider call side sets the worst case: its width less the credit, times 100, times 3.

deeper.trap: Using the narrower put side gives a loss that is too small. Schwab calls a condor with uneven sides unbalanced or skewed, and says it takes on a directional bias. Here the bigger loss sits on the call side, reached at or beyond the 120 strike at expiry.

wrong.$750: Uses the narrower put side. The wider side sets the max loss.
wrong.$3,000: Uses the wide side but forgets the 2.50 credit.
wrong.$3,750: Adds the 2.50 credit instead of taking it off.

questions.story: Your buddy sold an iron condor for 1.50 with a month to go. Next day the stock hasn't moved, but implied volatility jumps.
questions.q: What does his position show now, all else equal?
choices: A loss on paper
A gain on paper
Nothing until the stock moves
His max loss gets bigger
questions.why: A loss on paper. He's short options, and that's what negative vega means: rising implied volatility works against him. The options he sold just got pricier, so the condor costs more to buy back, even with the stock flat. His max loss doesn't change. The strikes and the credit set that. If volatility cools off, the paper loss shrinks. It's the vega lesson you already know, seen from the seller's chair.
questions.lesson_line: Condor sellers want volatility to fall. A jump costs them, even with the stock flat.

wrong.Nothing until the stock moves: Option prices move with implied volatility too, not just with the stock.
wrong.A gain on paper: That's the buyer's side. He sold the options, and higher volatility makes them pricier.
wrong.His max loss gets bigger: The strikes and the credit set the max loss. Volatility only moves the price inside it.

questions.simple: A paper loss, because higher implied volatility makes the options he sold cost more to buy back.

questions.q: A short iron condor still earns from time decay after the stock pushes out to one of its wings.
questions.why: False. Time pays the seller while the stock sits near or between the short strikes. Push it out toward a wing and that flips. Theta turns negative out there, so the position bleeds as expiry gets closer. That's why a condor is never set and forget. When the stock leans on a short strike, the seller has to manage it, not hope.
questions.lesson_line: Near the short strikes, time pays the seller. Out at a wing, time costs him.
questions.simple: False, decay helps only while the stock stays near the short strikes. Out at a wing, time works against the seller.

questions.story: Schwab's example from April 7, 2026: SPX near 6,560. Sell the 6,960 call, buy the 7,060 call. Sell the 6,160 put, buy the 6,060 put. Max profit is $2,915.
questions.q: What's the most this one condor can lose?
questions.why: $7,085. Each side is 100 points wide: 7,060 minus 6,960 on the calls, 6,160 minus 6,060 on the puts. SPX options pay $100 a point. So one full side is 100 times 100, or $10,000. Take off the $2,915 credit and you get 7,085, the same figure Schwab prints. Only one side can lose, so you never count both. Bigger numbers, same math.
questions.lesson_line: Index size, same math: one side's width times the multiplier, minus the credit.

wrong.$10,000: That's one side's full width. The $2,915 credit comes off it.
wrong.$14,170: That doubles the max loss. SPX can't be above 6,960 and below 6,160 at once.
wrong.$12,915: Adds the credit to the width. The $2,915 taken in cuts the loss.

questions.simple: $7,085, because only one side can lose: 100 points times $100 is $10,000, less the $2,915 credit.

deeper.example: Both sides here are 100 points wide, so either one sets the max loss. When the sides differ, Schwab uses the width of the widest spread minus the net credit.

reasons: computed key (calc) on a dated Schwab example

questions.q: Your iron condor's sides are each 5 points wide, and you collect 1.25. One max loss wipes out how many max wins?
questions.why: 3. You risk 5 minus 1.25 to make 1.25. One full loss erases three full wins.
questions.lesson_line: Before you sell a condor, know how many winners one max loss erases.

questions.story: A friend holds an iron condor: long 45 put, short 50 put, short 60 call, long 65 call. Expiration Friday, the stock closes at 61.50.
questions.q: If he does nothing, what's likely in his account Monday?
choices: Short 100 shares
No position at all
Long 100 shares
Short 200 shares
questions.why: Short 100 shares. At 61.50 the 60 call he sold is in the money, so he should expect assignment, though it's not guaranteed. The 65 call and both puts expire worthless. Assignment sells 100 shares short, and nothing covers them over the weekend. If the stock gaps up Monday, he eats it with no cap. The fix is simple: close the short call before Friday's close. You never want the weekend deciding your position.
questions.lesson_line: Near a short strike on expiry day, close it before the bell. Don't let the weekend decide.

wrong.Long 100 shares: That's what an assigned short put does. Here the call side finished in the money.
wrong.Short 200 shares: Only the 60 call is in the money. One condor, one assignment, 100 shares.
wrong.No position at all: Only the out-of-the-money legs expire. An in-the-money short call should be expected to be assigned.

questions.simple: Short 100 shares, because the 60 call finished in the money and will likely be assigned, while the 65 call expired.

deeper.trap: The weekend is the danger. You are short 100 shares with no long call above, so the short position is unhedged into Monday. The Options Industry Council warns a surprise at expiry can leave you long or short stock over the weekend. Closing the short call before the bell removes the guesswork.

questions.q: Most long butterflies held to expiry pay out their full max profit.
questions.why: False. The full payoff needs the stock to close exactly on the middle strike at expiry. The Options Industry Council calls that possible but statistically unlikely. A butterfly also shows little profit until close to expiry, and only with the stock near the center. Outside the wings, the debit's gone. So that tall peak on the payoff chart is the rare case. Judge one by its small, defined risk, not the peak.
questions.lesson_line: The peak on a butterfly's chart is the rare case. Judge it by the risk.
questions.simple: False, the full payoff needs a close right on the middle strike, and that's possible but rare.

deeper.example: Fidelity's example buys the 95 call, sells two 100 calls and buys the 105 call for 1.25. The 3.75 max profit needs a close at exactly 100. Above 105 or below 95 at expiry, the 1.25 is lost.

questions.story: A stock reports earnings tonight. Its options are pricey because implied volatility is high. A friend wants to sell an iron condor into the close.
questions.q: What has to happen for his trade to work?
choices: IV drops and the stock stays in range
IV drops, whatever the stock does
The stock gaps big in either direction
IV keeps rising after the report
questions.answer: IV drops and the stock stays in range
questions.why: IV drops and the stock stays in range. He needs both. Implied volatility tends to fall hard after a report, and that cheapens the condor he sold. But it only pays if the stock also lands between his break-evens. Gap too far either way and the IV drop won't save him. Schwab says most traders who sell condors on single stocks avoid earnings, because of outsized, unexpected moves. For us it's simpler: we don't make new buys right before a report.
questions.lesson_line: IV crush only pays if the stock stays inside the break-evens. Two bets, and he needs both.

wrong.IV drops, whatever the stock does: A big enough move beats the IV drop. Too far up or down is a loss.
wrong.The stock gaps big in either direction: That's what a straddle buyer wants. He sold the range, so a big gap is his loss.
wrong.IV keeps rising after the report: Rising IV hurts a short condor, and it tends to fall after the report anyway.

questions.simple: Implied volatility has to drop and the stock has to stay inside his break-evens, because a big gap beats the volatility drop.

deeper.trap: The IV drop and the price move are two separate bets, and you need to win both. Fidelity says success needs the stock to stay between the break-evens, and a move too far either way is a loss. Schwab says the trade can profit if the IV crush comes without significant movement in the stock.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09: lesson line credits Schwab)

questions.story: Ten days before expiry, the stock has dropped hard. Your iron condor's short put is now deep in the money. You get an assignment notice.
questions.q: What do you hold now?
choices: Long 100 shares plus three legs
Nothing, the condor is closed
Short 100 shares plus three legs
Max loss, booked automatically
questions.why: Long 100 shares plus three legs. You bought 100 shares at the put strike, and the long put and both calls are still open.
questions.lesson_line: Assignment breaks the condor into pieces. Deal with the shares and the leftover legs the same day.

wrong.Nothing, the condor is closed: Assignment fills one leg only. The other three stay open until you act.
wrong.Short 100 shares plus three legs: An assigned short call does that. An assigned put makes you buy the shares.
wrong.Max loss, booked automatically: Nothing is booked for you. You now own shares, and only your long put still limits the downside.

questions.q: A friend wants to sell condors with zero early assignment risk. Which options give him that?
choices: European-style index options, like SPX
American-style options on an index
Options on a stock with no dividend
Stock options sold far out of the money
questions.why: European-style index options, like SPX. Cboe says SPX options can only be exercised at expiration, so nobody can assign him early. They settle in cash too, so no shares ever land in his account. An American-style option can be exercised any day before expiry, whatever it's on. So the thing to check on a chain is the exercise style, not the underlying. It takes away early assignment, not the market risk.
questions.lesson_line: European-style can't be assigned before expiry. American-style can, any day.

wrong.American-style options on an index: Exercise style decides it, not the underlying. An American-style option can be exercised any day before expiry.
wrong.Options on a stock with no dividend: No dividend lowers the odds, but an American-style option can still be assigned early. Deep in-the-money puts often are.
wrong.Stock options sold far out of the money: Out of the money today can change. American-style shorts can be assigned any time, even some that expire out of the money.

questions.simple: European-style index options like SPX, because they can only be exercised at expiry, so nobody can assign him early.

deeper.counter: Out of the money is not protection. The stock can move and put your short option in the money. An American-style short can be assigned at any time before expiry. Fidelity notes early assignment of stock options is usually tied to dividends. No dividend lowers the odds but does not remove them. Deep in-the-money puts are often exercised early.

reasons: contract spec (exercise style) that could change; check Cboe's page

questions.story: A friend's condor got its short 50 put assigned, so he now owns 100 shares. The stock is at 44, and his long 45 put still has time value.
questions.q: What's the better way out?
choices: Sell the shares, then the long put
Exercise the long put right away
Hold the shares and wait for a bounce
Buy back the short put to undo it
questions.answer: Sell the shares, then the long put
questions.why: Sell the shares, then sell the long put. Exercising the 45 put would dump the shares at 45, but it throws away the time value still in the put. Sell the shares at 44, then sell the put in the market, and he collects that time value too. Fidelity prefers this two-step exit for that reason. Watch the fees on the extra trade, though. They can change the math. Same idea anytime you hold an option with time left: selling it beats exercising it.
questions.lesson_line: After an assignment, sell the leftover long option, don't exercise it. Selling keeps its time value.

wrong.Exercise the long put right away: That gets rid of the shares, but it throws away the put's time value.
wrong.Hold the shares and wait for a bounce: That turns a range trade into a stock trade nobody planned. Close what the assignment handed him.
wrong.Buy back the short put to undo it: The short put is gone. Assignment filled it, and only the long put and both calls are left.

questions.simple: Sell the shares, then sell the long put, because selling keeps the time value that exercising throws away.

deeper.trap: Exercising feels tidy: one step and the shares are gone at 45. But a put with time left is worth more than its exercise value. Exercising throws that extra away. Selling the put in the market captures its whole price.

questions.q: An iron condor's loss can never go past its stated max loss.
questions.why: False. The max loss assumes the four legs settle together. An early assignment before a dividend, or a pin at expiry, can leave you holding stock that moves against you.
questions.lesson_line: Defined risk holds only while all four legs stay together. Watch assignment and the closing bell.

questions.story: Your iron condor is up most of its credit with a week to expiry. The stock is drifting up toward your short call.
questions.q: What's the sound move?
choices: Close it and keep most of the credit
Hold to expiry for the last few cents
Sell the long call to pocket its value
questions.answer: Close it and keep most of the credit
questions.why: Close it and keep most of the credit. Near expiry, small stock moves swing a condor's price hard, and a close near the short call brings assignment risk.
questions.lesson_line: When most of the credit is in hand and expiry is close, I take it and move on.

wrong.Hold to expiry for the last few cents: That risks most of what you've made for a little more. Near expiry, small moves hit a condor hard.
wrong.Sell the long call to pocket its value: That leaves a naked short call, with no cap on the loss, right as the stock heads toward it.

conflicts: Naming: Fidelity says experienced traders disagree on whether the credit iron condor (and iron butterfly) is 'long' or 'short'; some call the credit trade a 'long iron condor'. OIC ('Short Condor (Iron Condor)', 'Short Iron Butterfly') and Schwab call the credit trade short and the debit trade long. The file says 'iron condor' or 'short iron condor' for the credit trade and never quizzes the long/short label.

OIC's August 2026 webinar uses 'a traditional long condor' for a four-call or four-put debit condor that profits between the inner strikes; OIC's own 'Long Condor' strategy page (and Schwab's 'long iron condor') is the debit trade that profits OUTSIDE the range. Checker: q01's wrong note now names the bull call + bear put pair 'the long iron condor' (Schwab f134) instead of 'OIC calls it a long condor', so the two OIC meanings never clash in front of a member.

Iron condor vs iron butterfly 'risk': OIC's October 2025 takeaways say the condor offers 'more flexibility and lower risk'; Fidelity's webinar deck says the condor has 'Less premium received, higher max loss'. Both hold in different senses (more room makes a loss less likely; less credit on the same wing width makes the max loss bigger). q08 keys only on credit and range, where both agree.

Unequal wings: OIC's formula assumes equal wings; Schwab says the max loss is the width of the widest spread minus the credit, which matches the Journal's compute_max_risk (wider wing x 100 x min qty + net entry). q15 keys Schwab (f122) with OIC's 'whichever are in-the-money' logic (f08) and a calc.

Earnings: Fidelity says some traders open condors immediately before earnings; Schwab says most traders who sell condors on single stocks avoid earnings. q22 keys only what both say (IV must fall AND the stock must stay inside the breakevens) and reports Schwab's 'most avoid' as Schwab's statement.

Where time decay flips: OIC (August 2026) says theta is positive while the stock stays 'near the short strikes' and flips toward the outer wings; Fidelity says theta turns negative once the stock moves 'outside the range of maximum profit' (past a short strike). q17's key (False) holds under both readings.
